In *Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers* [[1]](#ref-1) ([ICLR 2023](https://iclr.cc/)), [Zhou](https://yongchao98.github.io/) et al. (University of Toronto, Vector Institute, University of Waterloo) propose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE), a black-box search that uses one large language model (LLM) to write candidate natural-language instructions for a task, then selects the best via the zero-shot performance of a second LLM.

> By conditioning on natural language instructions, large language models (LLMs) have displayed impressive capabilities as general-purpose computers. However, task performance depends significantly on the quality of the prompt used to steer the model, and most effective prompts have been handcrafted by humans. Inspired by classical program synthesis and the human approach to prompt engineering, we propose *Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE)* for automatic instruction generation and selection. In our method, we *treat the instruction as the "program,"* optimized by searching over a pool of instruction candidates proposed by an LLM in order to maximize a chosen score function. To evaluate the quality of the selected instruction, we evaluate the zero-shot performance of another LLM following the selected instruction. Extensive experiments show that our automatically generated instructions outperform the prior LLM baseline by a large margin and achieve better or comparable performance to the instructions generated by human annotators on *24/24 Instruction Induction tasks and 17/21 curated BIG-Bench tasks*. We conduct extensive qualitative and quantitative analyses to explore the performance of APE. We show that APE-engineered prompts are able to improve few-shot learning performance (by simply prepending them to standard in-context learning prompts), *find better zero-shot chain-of-thought prompts*, as well as steer models toward truthfulness and/or informativeness.

## Methods

APE casts instruction design as a program-synthesis problem over natural-language programs. Given a small set of input-output demonstrations:

1. **Propose.** A proposer LLM generates candidate instructions in one of two ways:
    - **Forward generation** — "here are examples, write the instruction."
    - **Reverse infilling** — the proposer fills in an `<INSERT>` slot placed between inputs and outputs.

    Forward mode is the default and works on any pretrained LLM, but constrains the instruction to sit at the end of the prompt. Reverse mode requires a proposer with infilling capability (e.g., T5, GLM, InsertGPT, or InstructGPT's `<INSERT>` token) and lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt, which the authors find more flexible. The paper uses forward mode for the Instruction Induction experiments and reverse mode for BIG-Bench. The choice is the user's, not an algorithmic gate inside APE.
2. **Score.** Each candidate is run through an executor LLM on a held-out set; the score is task accuracy or log-probability of the correct output.
3. **(Optional) resample.** Monte Carlo resampling asks the proposer to generate semantically similar variants of the best candidates and re-scores them.
4. **Select.** The instruction with the highest score wins.

No fine-tuning is involved and the method treats both the proposer and the executor as black boxes.

## Results

The paper evaluates APE on the 24 NLP tasks from the Instruction Induction [[2]](#ref-2) benchmark [[2]](#ref-2), plus the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset and [TruthfulQA](/posts/20230226-truthfulqa-llm-truthfulness/) [[3]](#ref-3). It compares three sources of instructions:

- **APE** — the full propose-score-select pipeline.
- **Greedy** — Honovich et al.'s [[2]](#ref-2) prior algorithm, which takes the proposer's first sample without any selection step.
- **Human** — gold annotations written by the original Instruction Induction annotators.

With InstructGPT (175B) as both proposer and executor, APE reaches an interquartile mean of 0.810 across the 24 Instruction Induction tasks versus 0.749 for human-engineered prompts (Figure 1b), and achieves zero-shot accuracy at or above the human bar on all 24 of 24 individual tasks while the Greedy baseline trails on most (Figure 4). On the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset, APE matches or beats humans on 17 of 21 curated tasks. On TruthfulQA, APE-generated prompts steer the model toward truthful or informative outputs on demand, beating the human "help" prompt with 200 candidate proposals. Prepending APE prompts to few-shot in-context learning prompts also improves downstream performance on 21 of 24 tasks.

## My Notes

- **A benchmark designed to favor short prompts.** The 24-of-24 headline comes from Instruction Induction [[2]](#ref-2) tasks (singularize, translate, capitalize, etc.), which are short, template-shaped tasks where human prompt writers have little advantage. A crisp one-sentence instruction is close to the Bayes-optimal prompt, and LLMs can generate dozens of paraphrases of "output the plural form" cheaply. The result does not transfer to tasks where the useful prompt is paragraphs long, contains domain-specific scaffolding, or requires carefully chosen few-shot demonstrations. Later optimizers like MIPROv2 [[4]](#ref-4) and [GEPA](/posts/20260513-gepa/) [[5]](#ref-5) target that harder regime.
- **Reverse infilling, the transferable idea.** Forward generation ("here are examples, write the instruction") forces the instruction to be predicted at the end of the prompt, which is rarely where instructions naturally sit. The reverse infilling prompt, which feeds inputs on the left and outputs on the right and asks the model to fill in the instruction between them, lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt where it more naturally belongs. This matches what T5-style span corruption [[6]](#ref-6) showed about bidirectional objectives years earlier, and it sits in the same family as the [prompt-repetition trick](/posts/20260421-prompt-repetition/) for recovering bidirectional context inside a causal LM. Both are runtime workarounds for the fact that left-to-right generation can't condition on what comes after the token being predicted.
- **Scoring dominates the compute budget.** APE's compute is spent evaluating candidates on a held-out set with the executor LLM, not generating candidates with the proposer. The Monte Carlo resampling step, the only part of APE that resembles iterative optimization, does not add much over the base proposer pool for most tasks. The subsequent line of work (MIPROv2 [[4]](#ref-4) Bayesian surrogate, [GEPA](/posts/20260513-gepa/) [[5]](#ref-5) reflective mutation, [Promptbreeder](/posts/20260515-promptbreeder/) [[7]](#ref-7) evolutionary operators) all attack this scoring bottleneck with different mechanisms.
- **The thin human baseline.** The "human" prompts in the benchmark are typically one-sentence instructions written by a small number of annotators under Honovich et al.'s protocol [[2]](#ref-2), not prompts tuned by expert prompt engineers with access to the executor's failure modes. The paper's headline claim is more accurately read as "APE matches a single-shot human annotator on short template tasks." The gap to genuine prompt-engineering expertise on open-ended tasks is a separate question the paper does not answer.

## Related Posts

- [Promptbreeder: Self-Referential Self-Improvement Via Prompt Evolution](/posts/20260515-promptbreeder/): the direct successor that adds evolutionary operators on top of APE's propose-and-select loop.
- [EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers](/posts/20260430-evoprompt/): another gradient-free prompt search that benchmarks itself against APE and beats it on BIG-Bench Hard.
- [GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning](/posts/20260513-gepa/): the later optimizer that targets the harder, long-prompt regime APE's short-template benchmark leaves untouched.
- [DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines](/posts/20260430-dspy/): generalizes the "treat the prompt as the program to optimize" idea from a single instruction to a compiled multi-module pipeline.
- [Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs](/posts/20260421-prompt-repetition/): a sibling runtime workaround for the same causal-LM limitation that motivates APE's reverse-infilling mode.
